PROP
44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. Fiscal Impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
CON
Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. American Academy of Pediatrics CA, California Medical Association, California Academy of Family Physicians, California School Nurses Organization, doctors, nurses and patients urge NO on 44! www.NOProp44.com

PROP
44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. Fiscal Impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
CON
Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. American Academy of Pediatrics CA, California Medical Association, California Academy of Family Physicians, California School Nurses Organization, doctors, nurses and patients urge NO on 44! www.NOProp44.com

PROP
44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. Fiscal Impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
CON
Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. American Academy of Pediatrics CA, California Medical Association, California Academy of Family Physicians, California School Nurses Organization, doctors, nurses and patients urge NO on 44! www.NOProp44.com

Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local IN SUMMARY Proposition 44 would require clinics to spend more money on patient care. The union pushing the measure is the same one supporting the billionaire tax proposal. Clinics say the measure will force closures. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. The same union that put forward the billionaire wealth tax has another, lesser-known proposal on the ballot: Proposition 44 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-44-clinic-funding/). Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West wants voters to change how community health clinics spend money and penalize those that violate the ballot initiative’s provisions. The union claims too many clinics spend money inappropriately on things like high executive salaries rather than patient care. Clinics say they already prioritize patients and the initiative could bankrupt many facilities. While public interest in the billionaire tax fight dwarfs all other ballot measures, Prop. 44 is also shaping up to be contentious. Here’s what to know about it. What would the proposition do? Prop. 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/analysis.htm) would require community health clinics, known as federally qualified health centers, to spend 90% of their revenue on “program services” that advance their mission to provide charitable care to low-income and uninsured patients. The proposition would prohibit clinics from spending more than 10% of revenue on other things such as administrative expenses. It would also penalize clinics that don’t meet the new 90% spending threshold. The attorney general could fine clinics that don’t comply, and the money would go into a special fund reserved for health workforce spending. Community health clinics are nonprofits that are required by law to reinvest 100% of revenue back into the organization regardless of how voters decide on Prop. 44. Most clinics spend about 80% of revenue providing health services, although some spend less, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=44&year=2026). Just one in three likely voters support the initiative, according to a September poll from the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). Who supports it? SEIU-UHW is the primary proponent of the initiative and has raised about $17 million to support the campaign, mainly from union coffers. The union tried last year to get lawmakers to pass a bill to do nearly the same thing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1113), but it died in committee. The group argues that dramatic federal healthcare cuts targeting programs for low-income patients make it crucial for clinics to spend money on patient services rather than administrative or other costs. “We’re seeing clinics that have extravagant fundraisers or art collections or CEOs that are paid in the millions while their patients are struggling to get appointments, while the workers are dealing with broken equipment,” union spokesperson Renee Saldana said. Saldana said the initiative is meant to secure spending for patients and workers, not take money away from clinics. It would also allow clinics to earn penalty money back if they come into compliance. Who opposes it? Opponents include groups representing clinics, doctors and hospitals as well as the unlikely bedfellows of the California Democratic, Republican and Working Families parties. They’ve collectively raised about $37.6 million against the measure. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Sign up for free Δ Francisco Silva, chief executive of the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics, called the initiative an “existential threat.” Clinic spending is already highly regulated, Silva said, and the measure would force clinics to cut services, cut staff or close. Most clinics would pay a collective $1.7 billion in penalties in the first year and nearly half of all clinics in the state could close, according to a study commissioned by the primary care association (https://noprop44.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf). “In many communities, the community health center is the only source of care,” Silva said. “You’re going to be losing the basic safety net if you lose half of the community health centers.” Silva said that the initiative would prevent clinics from spending on things like patient navigators, translators and food pantries. It would also prevent clinics, he said, from investing in capital improvements like renovations and new buildings. The union disagrees and says the initiative allows the attorney general to decide what type of spending counts toward patient services. If the Legislature rejected this, why put it on the ballot? Special interest groups have used ballot initiatives — or the threat of them — to gain political leverage for decades, but perhaps no other group has done so more effectively or prolifically as SEIU-UHW (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/06/health-ballot-measures-deal-billionaires/). The union, which represents 120,000 healthcare workers, has successfully used ballot initiatives to secure deals in Sacramento. Its biggest achievement was a $25 per hour health worker minimum wage (https://calmatters.org/health/2023/09/california-minimum-wage-health-care-workers/) in 2023. But the primary care association alleges those practices violate anti-racketeering laws (https://www.legalnewsline.com/northern-california-record/union-uses-ca-ballot-initiatives-to-strongarm-clinics-lawsuit/article_7c623996-6763-48fc-88bf-65d50af60749.html). In a complaint filed in September in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California, the association and several clinics allege the union has unlawfully offered to kill Prop. 44 in exchange for more union membership at clinics or for the association to withdraw its opposition to the SEIU-UHW supported billionaire wealth tax. “Dave Regan and SEIU-UHW are extorting health centers by using the ballot measure process as as a way to get (the association) and health centers to agree to their demands that are entirely unrelated to Prop. 44,” said Joey Cachuela, general counsel for the primary care association, referencing the union’s president. Saldana said the allegations are “categorically false.” “This is the second time the (the association) has attempted to use legal filings to bully the healthcare workers of SEIU-UHW into backing down from holding clinics and CEOs accountable to patients,” she said. A judge dismissed a previous lawsuit filed by the primary care association to keep the initiative off the ballot. # Proposition 44
Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services.
Initiative Statute.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
These clinics currently report spending an average of about 80 percent of their revenue on providing health care services, though the percent varies across clinics.
### Proposal
***Sets Minimum Spending on Health Care at Private Nonprofit Safety Net Clinics.*** Proposition 44 requires private nonprofit safety net clinics to spend at least 90 percent of their total revenue each year on providing health care services.
This means that spending on other expenses, such as administrative costs, would be limited to no more than 10 percent of revenue.

The same union that put forward the billionaire wealth tax has another, lesser-known proposal on the ballot: Proposition 44 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-44-clinic-funding/). Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West wants voters to change how community health clinics spend money and penalize those that violate the ballot initiative’s provisions. The union claims too many clinics spend money inappropriately on things like high executive salaries rather than patient care. Clinics say they already prioritize patients and the initiative could bankrupt many facilities. While public interest in the billionaire tax fight dwarfs all other ballot measures, Prop. 44 is also shaping up to be contentious. Here’s what to know about it. What would the proposition do? Prop. 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/analysis.htm) would require community health clinics, known as federally qualified health centers, to spend 90% of their revenue on “program services” that advance their mission to provide charitable care to low-income and uninsured patients. The proposition would prohibit clinics from spending more than 10% of revenue on other things such as administrative expenses. It would also penalize clinics that don’t meet the new 90% spending threshold. The attorney general could fine clinics that don’t comply, and the money would go into a special fund reserved for health workforce spending. Community health clinics are nonprofits that are required by law to reinvest 100% of revenue back into the organization regardless of how voters decide on Prop. 44. Most clinics spend about 80% of revenue providing health services, although some spend less, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=44&year=2026). Just one in three likely voters support the initiative, according to a September poll from the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). Who supports it? SEIU-UHW is the primary proponent of the initiative and has raised about $17 million to support the campaign, mainly from union coffers. The union tried last year to get lawmakers to pass a bill to do nearly the same thing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1113), but it died in committee. The group argues that dramatic federal healthcare cuts targeting programs for low-income patients make it crucial for clinics to spend money on patient services rather than administrative or other costs. “We’re seeing clinics that have extravagant fundraisers or art collections or CEOs that are paid in the millions while their patients are struggling to get appointments, while the workers are dealing with broken equipment,” union spokesperson Renee Saldana said. Saldana said the initiative is meant to secure spending for patients and workers, not take money away from clinics. It would also allow clinics to earn penalty money back if they come into compliance. Who opposes it? Opponents include groups representing clinics, doctors and hospitals as well as the unlikely bedfellows of the California Democratic, Republican and Working Families parties. They’ve collectively raised about $37.6 million against the measure. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Sign up for free Δ Francisco Silva, chief executive of the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics, called the initiative an “existential threat.” Clinic spending is already highly regulated, Silva said, and the measure would force clinics to cut services, cut staff or close. Most clinics would pay a collective $1.7 billion in penalties in the first year and nearly half of all clinics in the state could close, according to a study commissioned by the primary care association (https://noprop44.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf). “In many communities, the community health center is the only source of care,” Silva said. “You’re going to be losing the basic safety net if you lose half of the community health centers.” Silva said that the initiative would prevent clinics from spending on things like patient navigators, translators and food pantries. It would also prevent clinics, he said, from investing in capital improvements like renovations and new buildings. The union disagrees and says the initiative allows the attorney general to decide what type of spending counts toward patient services. If the Legislature rejected this, why put it on the ballot? Special interest groups have used ballot initiatives — or the threat of them — to gain political leverage for decades, but perhaps no other group has done so more effectively or prolifically as SEIU-UHW (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/06/health-ballot-measures-deal-billionaires/). The union, which represents 120,000 healthcare workers, has successfully used ballot initiatives to secure deals in Sacramento. Its biggest achievement was a $25 per hour health worker minimum wage (https://calmatters.org/health/2023/09/california-minimum-wage-health-care-workers/) in 2023. But the primary care association alleges those practices violate anti-racketeering laws (https://www.legalnewsline.com/northern-california-record/union-uses-ca-ballot-initiatives-to-strongarm-clinics-lawsuit/article_7c623996-6763-48fc-88bf-65d50af60749.html). In a complaint filed in September in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California, the association and several clinics allege the union has unlawfully offered to kill Prop. 44 in exchange for more union membership at clinics or for the association to withdraw its opposition to the SEIU-UHW supported billionaire wealth tax. “Dave Regan and SEIU-UHW are extorting health centers by using the ballot measure process as as a way to get (the association) and health centers to agree to their demands that are entirely unrelated to Prop. 44,” said Joey Cachuela, general counsel for the primary care association, referencing the union’s president. Saldana said the allegations are “categorically false.” “This is the second time the (the association) has attempted to use legal filings to bully the healthcare workers of SEIU-UHW into backing down from holding clinics and CEOs accountable to patients,” she said. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local IN SUMMARY Proposition 44 would require clinics to spend more money on patient care. The union pushing the measure is the same one supporting the billionaire tax proposal. Clinics say the measure will force closures. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. The same union that put forward the billionaire wealth tax has another, lesser-known proposal on the ballot: Proposition 44 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-44-clinic-funding/). Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West wants voters to change how community health clinics spend money and penalize those that violate the ballot initiative’s provisions. The union claims too many clinics spend money inappropriately on things like high executive salaries rather than patient care. Clinics say they already prioritize patients and the initiative could bankrupt many facilities. While public interest in the billionaire tax fight dwarfs all other ballot measures, Prop. 44 is also shaping up to be contentious. Here’s what to know about it. What would the proposition do? Prop. 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/analysis.htm) would require community health clinics, known as federally qualified health centers, to spend 90% of their revenue on “program services” that advance their mission to provide charitable care to low-income and uninsured patients. The proposition would prohibit clinics from spending more than 10% of revenue on other things such as administrative expenses. It would also penalize clinics that don’t meet the new 90% spending threshold. The attorney general could fine clinics that don’t comply, and the money would go into a special fund reserved for health workforce spending. Community health clinics are nonprofits that are required by law to reinvest 100% of revenue back into the organization regardless of how voters decide on Prop. 44. Most clinics spend about 80% of revenue providing health services, although some spend less, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=44&year=2026). Just one in three likely voters support the initiative, according to a September poll from the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). Who supports it? SEIU-UHW is the primary proponent of the initiative and has raised about $17 million to support the campaign, mainly from union coffers. The union tried last year to get lawmakers to pass a bill to do nearly the same thing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1113), but it died in committee. The group argues that dramatic federal healthcare cuts targeting programs for low-income patients make it crucial for clinics to spend money on patient services rather than administrative or other costs. “We’re seeing clinics that have extravagant fundraisers or art collections or CEOs that are paid in the millions while their patients are struggling to get appointments, while the workers are dealing with broken equipment,” union spokesperson Renee Saldana said. Saldana said the initiative is meant to secure spending for patients and workers, not take money away from clinics. It would also allow clinics to earn penalty money back if they come into compliance. Who opposes it? Opponents include groups representing clinics, doctors and hospitals as well as the unlikely bedfellows of the California Democratic, Republican and Working Families parties. They’ve collectively raised about $37.6 million against the measure. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Francisco Silva, chief executive of the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics, called the initiative an “existential threat.” Clinic spending is already highly regulated, Silva said, and the measure would force clinics to cut services, cut staff or close. Most clinics would pay a collective $1.7 billion in penalties in the first year and nearly half of all clinics in the state could close, according to a study commissioned by the primary care association (https://noprop44.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf). “In many communities, the community health center is the only source of care,” Silva said. “You’re going to be losing the basic safety net if you lose half of the community health centers.” Silva said that the initiative would prevent clinics from spending on things like patient navigators, translators and food pantries. It would also prevent clinics, he said, from investing in capital improvements like renovations and new buildings. The union disagrees and says the initiative allows the attorney general to decide what type of spending counts toward patient services. If the Legislature rejected this, why put it on the ballot? Special interest groups have used ballot initiatives — or the threat of them — to gain political leverage for decades, but perhaps no other group has done so more effectively or prolifically as SEIU-UHW (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/06/health-ballot-measures-deal-billionaires/). The union, which represents 120,000 healthcare workers, has successfully used ballot initiatives to secure deals in Sacramento. Its biggest achievement was a $25 per hour health worker minimum wage (https://calmatters.org/health/2023/09/california-minimum-wage-health-care-workers/) in 2023. But the primary care association alleges those practices violate anti-racketeering laws (https://www.legalnewsline.com/northern-california-record/union-uses-ca-ballot-initiatives-to-strongarm-clinics-lawsuit/article_7c623996-6763-48fc-88bf-65d50af60749.html). In a complaint filed in September in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California, the association and several clinics allege the union has unlawfully offered to kill Prop. 44 in exchange for more union membership at clinics or for the association to withdraw its opposition to the SEIU-UHW supported billionaire wealth tax. “Dave Regan and SEIU-UHW are extorting health centers by using the ballot measure process as as a way to get (the association) and health centers to agree to their demands that are entirely unrelated to Prop. 44,” said Joey Cachuela, general counsel for the primary care association, referencing the union’s president. Saldana said the allegations are “categorically false.” “This is the second time the (the association) has attempted to use legal filings to bully the healthcare workers of SEIU-UHW into backing down from holding clinics and CEOs accountable to patients,” she said. A judge dismissed a previous lawsuit filed by the primary care association to keep the initiative off the ballot. ## Analysis of Measure
### Background
These clinics currently report spending an average of about 80 percent of their revenue on providing health care services, though the percent varies across clinics.
### Proposal
***Sets Minimum Spending on Health Care at Private Nonprofit Safety Net Clinics.*** Proposition 44 requires private nonprofit safety net clinics to spend at least 90 percent of their total revenue each year on providing health care services.
This means that spending on other expenses, such as administrative costs, would be limited to no more than 10 percent of revenue.
The California Attorney General would define in more detail which kinds of expenses are related to providing health care services, and which are other expenses, using existing reports to the federal government as a starting point.
Affected clinics could ask the state for a temporary waiver of the requirements in some cases.
***Creates Penalty for Falling Short of Minimum.*** Proposition 44 requires affected clinics to pay a penalty to the state if they fall short of the new health care spending minimum.
The penalty would equal the amount of spending needed to reach the 90 percent minimum.
Clinics could get their money back if they comply with the spending requirements within five years.

On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot.
It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services.
No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services.
The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall.
The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years.
If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.

The same union that put forward the billionaire wealth tax has another, lesser-known proposal on the ballot: Proposition 44 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-44-clinic-funding/). Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West wants voters to change how community health clinics spend money and penalize those that violate the ballot initiative’s provisions. The union claims too many clinics spend money inappropriately on things like high executive salaries rather than patient care. Clinics say they already prioritize patients and the initiative could bankrupt many facilities. While public interest in the billionaire tax fight dwarfs all other ballot measures, Prop. 44 is also shaping up to be contentious. Here’s what to know about it. What would the proposition do? Prop. 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/analysis.htm) would require community health clinics, known as federally qualified health centers, to spend 90% of their revenue on “program services” that advance their mission to provide charitable care to low-income and uninsured patients. The proposition would prohibit clinics from spending more than 10% of revenue on other things such as administrative expenses. It would also penalize clinics that don’t meet the new 90% spending threshold. The attorney general could fine clinics that don’t comply, and the money would go into a special fund reserved for health workforce spending. Community health clinics are nonprofits that are required by law to reinvest 100% of revenue back into the organization regardless of how voters decide on Prop. 44. Most clinics spend about 80% of revenue providing health services, although some spend less, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=44&year=2026). Just one in three likely voters support the initiative, according to a September poll from the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). Who supports it? SEIU-UHW is the primary proponent of the initiative and has raised about $17 million to support the campaign, mainly from union coffers. The union tried last year to get lawmakers to pass a bill to do nearly the same thing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1113), but it died in committee. The group argues that dramatic federal healthcare cuts targeting programs for low-income patients make it crucial for clinics to spend money on patient services rather than administrative or other costs. “We’re seeing clinics that have extravagant fundraisers or art collections or CEOs that are paid in the millions while their patients are struggling to get appointments, while the workers are dealing with broken equipment,” union spokesperson Renee Saldana said. Saldana said the initiative is meant to secure spending for patients and workers, not take money away from clinics. It would also allow clinics to earn penalty money back if they come into compliance. Who opposes it? Opponents include groups representing clinics, doctors and hospitals as well as the unlikely bedfellows of the California Democratic, Republican and Working Families parties. They’ve collectively raised about $37.6 million against the measure. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Sign up for free Δ Francisco Silva, chief executive of the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics, called the initiative an “existential threat.” Clinic spending is already highly regulated, Silva said, and the measure would force clinics to cut services, cut staff or close. Most clinics would pay a collective $1.7 billion in penalties in the first year and nearly half of all clinics in the state could close, according to a study commissioned by the primary care association (https://noprop44.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf). “In many communities, the community health center is the only source of care,” Silva said. “You’re going to be losing the basic safety net if you lose half of the community health centers.” Silva said that the initiative would prevent clinics from spending on things like patient navigators, translators and food pantries. It would also prevent clinics, he said, from investing in capital improvements like renovations and new buildings. The union disagrees and says the initiative allows the attorney general to decide what type of spending counts toward patient services. If the Legislature rejected this, why put it on the ballot? Special interest groups have used ballot initiatives — or the threat of them — to gain political leverage for decades, but perhaps no other group has done so more effectively or prolifically as SEIU-UHW (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/06/health-ballot-measures-deal-billionaires/). The union, which represents 120,000 healthcare workers, has successfully used ballot initiatives to secure deals in Sacramento. Its biggest achievement was a $25 per hour health worker minimum wage (https://calmatters.org/health/2023/09/california-minimum-wage-health-care-workers/) in 2023. But the primary care association alleges those practices violate anti-racketeering laws (https://www.legalnewsline.com/northern-california-record/union-uses-ca-ballot-initiatives-to-strongarm-clinics-lawsuit/article_7c623996-6763-48fc-88bf-65d50af60749.html). In a complaint filed in September in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California, the association and several clinics allege the union has unlawfully offered to kill Prop. 44 in exchange for more union membership at clinics or for the association to withdraw its opposition to the SEIU-UHW supported billionaire wealth tax. “Dave Regan and SEIU-UHW are extorting health centers by using the ballot measure process as as a way to get (the association) and health centers to agree to their demands that are entirely unrelated to Prop. 44,” said Joey Cachuela, general counsel for the primary care association, referencing the union’s president. Saldana said the allegations are “categorically false.” “This is the second time the (the association) has attempted to use legal filings to bully the healthcare workers of SEIU-UHW into backing down from holding clinics and CEOs accountable to patients,” she said. A judge dismissed a previous lawsuit filed by the primary care association to keep the initiative off the ballot. 44
REQUIRES COMMUNITY HEALTH CLINICS SPEND 90% OF REVENUE ON PROGRAM SERVICES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. Fiscal Impact: Increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: American Academy of Pediatrics CA; CA School Nurses Org; CA Academy of Family Physicians; CA Medical Assoc.
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain private nonprofit health care clinics would have to spend at least 90 percent of their revenue each year on providing health care services.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The new requirement on health care clinic spending would not go into effect.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Prop. 44 holds community clinics and their executives accountable by requiring that 90% of clinic revenue be spent on clinics’ charitable mission: patient care and services that make care possible. It increases transparency, reduces wasteful executive spending, and ensures healthcare dollars go where they belong: caring for Californians in need.
CON
Prop. 44 is a dangerous measure that will shut down hundreds of community health clinics and eliminate vital patient services for millions of Californians. Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services.
Initiative Statute.
## Analysis of Measure
### Background
These clinics currently report spending an average of about 80 percent of their revenue on providing health care services, though the percent varies across clinics.
### Proposal
***Sets Minimum Spending on Health Care at Private Nonprofit Safety Net Clinics.*** Proposition 44 requires private nonprofit safety net clinics to spend at least 90 percent of their total revenue each year on providing health care services.
This means that spending on other expenses, such as administrative costs, would be limited to no more than 10 percent of revenue.
The California Attorney General would define in more detail which kinds of expenses are related to providing health care services, and which are other expenses, using existing reports to the federal government as a starting point.
Affected clinics could ask the state for a temporary waiver of the requirements in some cases.
***Creates Penalty for Falling Short of Minimum.*** Proposition 44 requires affected clinics to pay a penalty to the state if they fall short of the new health care spending minimum.
The penalty would equal the amount of spending needed to reach the 90 percent minimum.
Clinics could get their money back if they comply with the spending requirements within five years.

### Summary
On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot.
It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services.
No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services.
The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall.
The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years.
If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.

The same union that put forward the billionaire wealth tax has another, lesser-known proposal on the ballot: Proposition 44 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-44-clinic-funding/). Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West wants voters to change how community health clinics spend money and penalize those that violate the ballot initiative’s provisions. The union claims too many clinics spend money inappropriately on things like high executive salaries rather than patient care. Clinics say they already prioritize patients and the initiative could bankrupt many facilities. While public interest in the billionaire tax fight dwarfs all other ballot measures, Prop. 44 is also shaping up to be contentious. Here’s what to know about it. What would the proposition do? Prop. 44 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/44/analysis.htm) would require community health clinics, known as federally qualified health centers, to spend 90% of their revenue on “program services” that advance their mission to provide charitable care to low-income and uninsured patients. The proposition would prohibit clinics from spending more than 10% of revenue on other things such as administrative expenses. It would also penalize clinics that don’t meet the new 90% spending threshold. The attorney general could fine clinics that don’t comply, and the money would go into a special fund reserved for health workforce spending. Community health clinics are nonprofits that are required by law to reinvest 100% of revenue back into the organization regardless of how voters decide on Prop. 44. Most clinics spend about 80% of revenue providing health services, although some spend less, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=44&year=2026). Just one in three likely voters support the initiative, according to a September poll from the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). Who supports it? SEIU-UHW is the primary proponent of the initiative and has raised about $17 million to support the campaign, mainly from union coffers. The union tried last year to get lawmakers to pass a bill to do nearly the same thing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1113), but it died in committee. The group argues that dramatic federal healthcare cuts targeting programs for low-income patients make it crucial for clinics to spend money on patient services rather than administrative or other costs. “We’re seeing clinics that have extravagant fundraisers or art collections or CEOs that are paid in the millions while their patients are struggling to get appointments, while the workers are dealing with broken equipment,” union spokesperson Renee Saldana said. Saldana said the initiative is meant to secure spending for patients and workers, not take money away from clinics. It would also allow clinics to earn penalty money back if they come into compliance. Who opposes it? Opponents include groups representing clinics, doctors and hospitals as well as the unlikely bedfellows of the California Democratic, Republican and Working Families parties. They’ve collectively raised about $37.6 million against the measure. Just the right amount of news Just the right amount of news Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Sign up for free Δ Francisco Silva, chief executive of the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics, called the initiative an “existential threat.” Clinic spending is already highly regulated, Silva said, and the measure would force clinics to cut services, cut staff or close. Most clinics would pay a collective $1.7 billion in penalties in the first year and nearly half of all clinics in the state could close, according to a study commissioned by the primary care association (https://noprop44.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/BRG-Report-on-Clinic-Funding-Accountability-Transparency-Act-2025_1117.pdf). “In many communities, the community health center is the only source of care,” Silva said. “You’re going to be losing the basic safety net if you lose half of the community health centers.” Silva said that the initiative would prevent clinics from spending on things like patient navigators, translators and food pantries. It would also prevent clinics, he said, from investing in capital improvements like renovations and new buildings. The union disagrees and says the initiative allows the attorney general to decide what type of spending counts toward patient services. If the Legislature rejected this, why put it on the ballot? Special interest groups have used ballot initiatives — or the threat of them — to gain political leverage for decades, but perhaps no other group has done so more effectively or prolifically as SEIU-UHW (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/06/health-ballot-measures-deal-billionaires/). The union, which represents 120,000 healthcare workers, has successfully used ballot initiatives to secure deals in Sacramento. Its biggest achievement was a $25 per hour health worker minimum wage (https://calmatters.org/health/2023/09/california-minimum-wage-health-care-workers/) in 2023. But the primary care association alleges those practices violate anti-racketeering laws (https://www.legalnewsline.com/northern-california-record/union-uses-ca-ballot-initiatives-to-strongarm-clinics-lawsuit/article_7c623996-6763-48fc-88bf-65d50af60749.html). In a complaint filed in September in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California, the association and several clinics allege the union has unlawfully offered to kill Prop. 44 in exchange for more union membership at clinics or for the association to withdraw its opposition to the SEIU-UHW supported billionaire wealth tax. “Dave Regan and SEIU-UHW are extorting health centers by using the ballot measure process as as a way to get (the association) and health centers to agree to their demands that are entirely unrelated to Prop. 44,” said Joey Cachuela, general counsel for the primary care association, referencing the union’s president. Saldana said the allegations are “categorically false.” “This is the second time the (the association) has attempted to use legal filings to bully the healthcare workers of SEIU-UHW into backing down from holding clinics and CEOs accountable to patients,” she said. A judge dismissed a previous lawsuit filed by the primary care association to keep the initiative off the ballot. Election Results - November 3, 2026
California voters are casting their ballots for or against Proposition 40, a one-time tax on certain taxpayers with covered assets over $1 billion, with revenue primarily directed toward healthcare and portions toward food assistance or education-related programs. This page includes the latest results for Prop. 40, as well as other races in the Sacramento area.

California Prop 1 | Affordable Housing Bond (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/elections/california-prop-1-affordable-housing-bond/103-e7aca3bf-604e-443b-be82-fefddf278b4a)
Prop. 1 would allow $11.25 billion in bonds for housing programs and veterans’ home loans. (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/elections/california-prop-1-affordable-housing-bond/103-e7aca3bf-604e-443b-be82-fefddf278b4a)

### Summary
On May 18, 2026, the Secretary of State determined through a random sample that the measure had enough valid signatures to become eligible for the ballot.
It was formally certified for the November 3, 2026, statewide ballot on June 25, 2026, and subsequently designated Proposition 44.
Proposition 44 would require certain private nonprofit safety net clinics in California to spend at least 90% of their total revenue each year on providing health care services.
No more than 10% could be spent on administrative and other expenses that do not qualify as health care services.
The California Attorney General would establish more comprehensive rules for determining which expenses count toward the 90% requirement, and affected clinics could seek temporary waivers in certain circumstances.
Clinics that fail to meet the 90% spending requirement would have to pay a penalty to the state for an amount equal to the shortfall.
The clinic could be reimbursed if it comes into compliance within five years.
If it does not meet the requirements, the state would keep the money and use it to support workforce programs for safety net clinics.

A forgotten ballot measure? Union behind billionaire tax spends little on Prop. 44
By Ben Paviour
October 19, 2026 5:00 AM
Critics of Proposition 44 hold signs at a meeting of the resolutions committee of the California Democratic Party’s Executive Committee on Aug. 1, 2026. The measure would place new restrictions on how California’s federally-funded healthcare clinics spend money.
Ben Paviour
ben.paviour@sacbee.com
The union that put the billionaire tax on the ballot has put little money behind its other measure, Proposition 44 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317016992.html), a low-polling measure focused on health clinic spending.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West spent a little more than $20,000 on Prop. 44 from July 1 to Sept. 19, according to its most recent campaign filings, while opponents spent more than $32 million in the same period.
The SEIU-UHW appears to have concentrated its limited resources onProp. 40, a nationally-watched effort (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317075667.html) to impose a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth to offset federal healthcare cuts. The “Yes on 40” campaign spent $4.4 million during the period — still less than 10% of the total spent by billionaire tax opponents.
A Public Policy Institute of California poll released in mid-September (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) found Prop. 44 was the least popular propositions surveyed, with 34% of likely voters saying they supported the measure. Prop. 40, on the other hand, showed 52% support, though subsequent surveys have showed lower levels of support.
Prop. 44 would require federally-funded health clinics to spend 90% of their revenues on patient services, a move SEIU-UHW says would strengthen accountability. Critics like the California Primary Care Association argue the measure is poorly designed and was sponsored by SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan to win concessions from clinics SEIU-UHW is seeking to unionize.
Last month, the CPCA and five clinics filed a lawsuit accusing Regan and his union of racketeering. They argued he launches “punitive, harmful, and often long-shot and repetitive statewide or local ballot initiatives that are used as bargaining chips to extort broad concessions.” The case has yet to be heard.
The CPCA filed a lawsuit in April seeking to keep Prop. 44 off the ballot. A federal judge dismissed the case in August, saying the plaintiffs lacked standing.
Loading…
SEIU-UHW spokesperson Renée Saldaña said the union had not abandoned Prop. 44 and denied that bringing it was a negotiating tactic, calling the allegations in the latest lawsuit “categorically false.”
“Our path to victory is making sure voters understand what Prop 44 does: with federal cuts putting enormous pressure on California’s healthcare system, it ensures clinics that receive public funding spend that money on patient care,” Saldaña said. “SEIU-UHW members will be making that case through Election Day.”
No on 44 spokesperson Molly Weedn said they remained committed to defeating the measure.
“It’s shameful that UHW would put such a dangerous measure on the ballot and force community clinics to mount a campaign to defeat it, especially when there is so much work to do in communities ensuring people are getting the healthcare they need and deserve,” Weedn said in an email.

For 178 years, AP has been the steady voice America turns to on election night. Our reporters, election analysts and graphics journalists simply tell you who won — no spin, no bias, just facts. We're not owned by billionaires. We don't have an editorial agenda. We just count votes and report results, the same way we've done since 1848. Results are reported as soon as they are available. How this is built
Proposition 44 is forecast as a health care measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. How this is built
Proposition 44 is forecast as a health care measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). A forgotten ballot measure? Union behind billionaire tax spends little on Prop. 44
By Ben Paviour
October 19, 2026 5:00 AM
Critics of Proposition 44 hold signs at a meeting of the resolutions committee of the California Democratic Party’s Executive Committee on Aug. 1, 2026. The measure would place new restrictions on how California’s federally-funded healthcare clinics spend money.
Ben Paviour
ben.paviour@sacbee.com
The union that put the billionaire tax on the ballot has put little money behind its other measure, Proposition 44 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317016992.html), a low-polling measure focused on health clinic spending.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West spent a little more than $20,000 on Prop. 44 from July 1 to Sept. 19, according to its most recent campaign filings, while opponents spent more than $32 million in the same period.
The SEIU-UHW appears to have concentrated its limited resources onProp. 40, a nationally-watched effort (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317075667.html) to impose a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth to offset federal healthcare cuts. The “Yes on 40” campaign spent $4.4 million during the period — still less than 10% of the total spent by billionaire tax opponents.
A Public Policy Institute of California poll released in mid-September (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) found Prop. 44 was the least popular propositions surveyed, with 34% of likely voters saying they supported the measure. Prop. 40, on the other hand, showed 52% support, though subsequent surveys have showed lower levels of support.
Prop. 44 would require federally-funded health clinics to spend 90% of their revenues on patient services, a move SEIU-UHW says would strengthen accountability. Critics like the California Primary Care Association argue the measure is poorly designed and was sponsored by SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan to win concessions from clinics SEIU-UHW is seeking to unionize.
Last month, the CPCA and five clinics filed a lawsuit accusing Regan and his union of racketeering. They argued he launches “punitive, harmful, and often long-shot and repetitive statewide or local ballot initiatives that are used as bargaining chips to extort broad concessions.” The case has yet to be heard.
The CPCA filed a lawsuit in April seeking to keep Prop. 44 off the ballot. A federal judge dismissed the case in August, saying the plaintiffs lacked standing.
Loading…
SEIU-UHW spokesperson Renée Saldaña said the union had not abandoned Prop. 44 and denied that bringing it was a negotiating tactic, calling the allegations in the latest lawsuit “categorically false.”
“Our path to victory is making sure voters understand what Prop 44 does: with federal cuts putting enormous pressure on California’s healthcare system, it ensures clinics that receive public funding spend that money on patient care,” Saldaña said. “SEIU-UHW members will be making that case through Election Day.”
No on 44 spokesperson Molly Weedn said they remained committed to defeating the measure.
“It’s shameful that UHW would put such a dangerous measure on the ballot and force community clinics to mount a campaign to defeat it, especially when there is so much work to do in communities ensuring people are getting the healthcare they need and deserve,” Weedn said in an email.

The union that put the billionaire tax on the ballot has put little money behind its other measure, Proposition 44 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317016992.html), a low-polling measure focused on health clinic spending.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West spent a little more than $20,000 on Prop. 44 from July 1 to Sept. 19, according to its most recent campaign filings, while opponents spent more than $32 million in the same period.
The SEIU-UHW appears to have concentrated its limited resources onProp. 40, a nationally-watched effort (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317075667.html) to impose a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth to offset federal healthcare cuts. The “Yes on 40” campaign spent $4.4 million during the period — still less than 10% of the total spent by billionaire tax opponents.
A Public Policy Institute of California poll released in mid-September (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) found Prop. 44 was the least popular propositions surveyed, with 34% of likely voters saying they supported the measure. Prop. 40, on the other hand, showed 52% support, though subsequent surveys have showed lower levels of support.
Prop. 44 would require federally-funded health clinics to spend 90% of their revenues on patient services, a move SEIU-UHW says would strengthen accountability. Critics like the California Primary Care Association argue the measure is poorly designed and was sponsored by SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan to win concessions from clinics SEIU-UHW is seeking to unionize.
Last month, the CPCA and five clinics filed a lawsuit accusing Regan and his union of racketeering. They argued he launches “punitive, harmful, and often long-shot and repetitive statewide or local ballot initiatives that are used as bargaining chips to extort broad concessions.” The case has yet to be heard.
The CPCA filed a lawsuit in April seeking to keep Prop. 44 off the ballot. A federal judge dismissed the case in August, saying the plaintiffs lacked standing.
Loading…
SEIU-UHW spokesperson Renée Saldaña said the union had not abandoned Prop. 44 and denied that bringing it was a negotiating tactic, calling the allegations in the latest lawsuit “categorically false.”
“Our path to victory is making sure voters understand what Prop 44 does: with federal cuts putting enormous pressure on California’s healthcare system, it ensures clinics that receive public funding spend that money on patient care,” Saldaña said. “SEIU-UHW members will be making that case through Election Day.”
No on 44 spokesperson Molly Weedn said they remained committed to defeating the measure.
“It’s shameful that UHW would put such a dangerous measure on the ballot and force community clinics to mount a campaign to defeat it, especially when there is so much work to do in communities ensuring people are getting the healthcare they need and deserve,” Weedn said in an email.

How this is built
Proposition 44 is forecast as a health care measure whose Yes vote leans to neither party . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. A forgotten ballot measure? Union behind billionaire tax spends little on Prop. 44
By Ben Paviour
October 19, 2026 5:00 AM
Critics of Proposition 44 hold signs at a meeting of the resolutions committee of the California Democratic Party’s Executive Committee on Aug. 1, 2026. The measure would place new restrictions on how California’s federally-funded healthcare clinics spend money.
Ben Paviour
ben.paviour@sacbee.com
The union that put the billionaire tax on the ballot has put little money behind its other measure, Proposition 44 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317016992.html), a low-polling measure focused on health clinic spending.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West spent a little more than $20,000 on Prop. 44 from July 1 to Sept. 19, according to its most recent campaign filings, while opponents spent more than $32 million in the same period.
The SEIU-UHW appears to have concentrated its limited resources onProp. 40, a nationally-watched effort (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317075667.html) to impose a one-time, 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth to offset federal healthcare cuts. The “Yes on 40” campaign spent $4.4 million during the period — still less than 10% of the total spent by billionaire tax opponents.
A Public Policy Institute of California poll released in mid-September (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) found Prop. 44 was the least popular propositions surveyed, with 34% of likely voters saying they supported the measure. Prop. 40, on the other hand, showed 52% support, though subsequent surveys have showed lower levels of support.
Prop. 44 would require federally-funded health clinics to spend 90% of their revenues on patient services, a move SEIU-UHW says would strengthen accountability. Critics like the California Primary Care Association argue the measure is poorly designed and was sponsored by SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan to win concessions from clinics SEIU-UHW is seeking to unionize.
Last month, the CPCA and five clinics filed a lawsuit accusing Regan and his union of racketeering. They argued he launches “punitive, harmful, and often long-shot and repetitive statewide or local ballot initiatives that are used as bargaining chips to extort broad concessions.” The case has yet to be heard.
The CPCA filed a lawsuit in April seeking to keep Prop. 44 off the ballot. A federal judge dismissed the case in August, saying the plaintiffs lacked standing.
Loading…
SEIU-UHW spokesperson Renée Saldaña said the union had not abandoned Prop. 44 and denied that bringing it was a negotiating tactic, calling the allegations in the latest lawsuit “categorically false.”
“Our path to victory is making sure voters understand what Prop 44 does: with federal cuts putting enormous pressure on California’s healthcare system, it ensures clinics that receive public funding spend that money on patient care,” Saldaña said. “SEIU-UHW members will be making that case through Election Day.”
No on 44 spokesperson Molly Weedn said they remained committed to defeating the measure.
“It’s shameful that UHW would put such a dangerous measure on the ballot and force community clinics to mount a campaign to defeat it, especially when there is so much work to do in communities ensuring people are getting the healthcare they need and deserve,” Weedn said in an email.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
